screens.title: Solidity Data Types and Variables
screens.subtitle: Foundations for secure, gas-aware smart contracts

narration.text: In this lesson we'll build a firm understanding of Solidity's data types and variables, because every secure smart contract depends on choosing the right type and visibility. You will learn the practical difference between value types, which copy data, and reference types, which point to a location in memory or storage. We'll show why integers, addresses, byte arrays, enums, structs, arrays and mappings behave differently and how those behaviors affect gas use and security. For example, value types are cheap to copy but reference types can become expensive if you duplicate large arrays. You'll also see how visibility specifiers such as public, private, internal and external change who can call a function or read a variable, which directly impacts your attack surface. By the end of this module you will be able to pick efficient storage patterns and limit exposure with restrictive visibility. A concrete use case you will follow is a small UserProfile contract: it uses a struct and mapping to store profiles, and demonstrates create, update and read operations while showing typical revert checks. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions, like assuming mappings are iterable or that an address can receive Ether without being marked payable. Ready to explore the details and hands-on code that make contracts robust?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Choosing between value and reference types and setting correct visibility are essential to correctness, gas efficiency, and contract security.

Why it matters

Type choices affect storage cost, gas, and correctness. Visibility limits attack surface and unintended reads or calls.

Quick orientation
  • Value types: copied on assignment and cheap for small data.
  • Reference types: point to memory/storage and can be costly to copy.
  • Visibility: public/private/internal/external determine access and generated getters.
Concept visual
A value stores the data; a reference points to storage or memory.

Visibility & Security — public, private, internal, external

These topics define how data is stored, accessed, and how much gas operations cost.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of these exercises you will confidently choose and declare Solidity types, use reference structures safely, and apply visibility rules to protect state. First, you will learn to distinguish value types from reference types, which is essential because copying and referencing data have very different gas and correctness implications. Second, you will be able to declare and initialize core value types like unsigned and signed integers, booleans, Ethereum addresses, and byte arrays, and understand when to prefer fixed-size bytes for efficiency. Third, you will construct and use reference types—arrays, structs, and mappings—to model complex state and recognize patterns for safe updates. Finally, you will apply visibility specifiers to variables and functions, limiting access and minimizing your contract's attack surface. Each objective includes a short verification milestone so you can confirm competency as you work through the UserProfile example. These skills reduce bugs, improve gas efficiency, and make contracts easier to audit. Keep each milestone in mind as a concrete check of your knowledge during the hands-on lab.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.subtitle: Hands-on checks and common pitfalls to avoid

narration.text: These practice objectives focus on safe patterns and common pitfalls. You will implement a small UserProfile contract that stores and updates profiles, which verifies your understanding of structs and mappings. During the implementation you will practice guard clauses using require to avoid duplicate profiles and to ensure state exists before updating. You will also inspect gas implications: iterating over large arrays is expensive, and mappings do not list keys automatically. A typical safe pattern is to use mapping for O(1) checks and keep an optional array of keys for iteration when needed, accepting the extra gas cost. Finally, we will verify behavior under Solidity 0.8’s arithmetic checks so you see how overflow and underflow revert transactions by default. Each practice objective concludes with a small test: create a user, update a field, and trigger a require failure to observe the revert. These tests turn abstract rules into concrete expectations while teaching why those rules exist.

screens.title: Value Types vs Reference Types
screens.subtitle: Definition, semantics, and why the distinction matters

narration.text: Understanding the distinction between value and reference types is the first practical step toward writing predictable Solidity code. Value types store the data directly in the variable. When you assign a value type or pass it into a function, Solidity copies that data into the new variable or stack slot. This makes reasoning about simple items like booleans, integers, and addresses straightforward because each variable has its own independent value. Reference types, however, store a pointer to data that lives in memory or contract storage. Assigning or passing a reference type copies the pointer, so multiple variables can refer to the same underlying data. That shared reference means an update through one variable can affect others — which is powerful, but also a source of bugs and extra gas costs if you copy large structures unintentionally. A concrete example: passing a dynamic array by storage reference lets you append elements and persist them, while copying a large array into memory for local edits can be expensive. A common misconception is to assume mappings are iterable like arrays; they are not — mappings are reference-like and only store key-value relationships without length. Key takeaway: prefer value types for small independent data and use reference types when you need shared, structured state, but be deliberate about copies, storage location, and gas implications. What data will your contract store long-term, and how often will you read or write it?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Value types copy data; reference types copy pointers. This affects correctness and gas.

content.html:
Core Concept

Value vs Reference Types

A precise definition and practical implications for storage and gas.

Value types copy data: integer, bool, address.
Reference types copy pointers: arrays, structs, mappings.
Storage location matters: storage, memory, calldata.
Key Takeaway

Pick value types for independent small data. Use reference types intentionally and avoid copying large structures.

Example
// Storage reference vs memory copy
uint[] public storageArray;

function addThenCopy() public {
  storageArray.push(1); // modifies storage
  uint[] memory copyArray = storageArray; // copies values into memory -- gas cost
  // modifying copyArray does not change storageArray
}
Misconception

Assuming a reference assignment makes an independent snapshot. In reality you still reference the same storage unless you explicitly copy to memory.

screens.title: Common Value Types
screens.subtitle: bool, uint, int, address, bytes, string and enum usage

narration.text: Value types are the simplest building blocks in Solidity. Start with boolean, which stores true or false and is commonly used for flags. Unsigned and signed integers—uint and int—come in sizes from 8 to 256 bits; if you don't specify a size, Solidity defaults to 256 bits. Use uint256 for balances and counters because it matches the EVM word size and avoids surprises. Keep in mind integer overflow and underflow risks: in Solidity 0.8 and above standard arithmetic operations revert on overflow, preventing the classic wrap-around vulnerability unless you explicitly mark operations as unchecked. The address type holds 20-byte account identifiers; to send Ether you must use address payable or cast an address to payable. bytes and string handle binary data and text respectively; prefer fixed-size bytes for known-length data to save gas. Enums create named integer constants and improve readability of state values. A concrete example: use an enum to track an approval workflow state rather than numeric codes, making code clearer for auditors. Common mistakes include storing long strings on-chain—gas cost rises quickly—and assuming smaller integer sizes automatically save gas in all contexts. Choose types with a balance of clarity, correctness, and gas efficiency.

keyIdea.title: Practical note
keyIdea.text: Pick the smallest readable type that meets safety and EVM word alignment; prefer uint256 for balances.

content.html:
Value Types

bool · uint · int · address · bytes · string · enum

bool — flags, true or false.
uint / int — numeric types; default to 256 bits if unspecified.
address — 20-byte account or contract reference; cast to payable to send Ether.
bytes / string — binary and text; prefer bytes1..bytes32 if fixed length known.
enum — named integer states for readability.
Examples
bool isActive = true;
uint256 balance = 1000;
int256 temperature = -5;
address owner = 0xAbc1230000000000000000000000000000000000;
bytes32 myHash = keccak256("hello");
enum State { Pending, Approved, Rejected }

      

        
Misconception

        
Smaller bit widths always save gas—this is not always true. Choose types for clarity and safety; optimize only after measuring gas usage in context.

screens.title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
screens.subtitle: How Solidity 0.8+ handles arithmetic and what to watch for

narration.text: Integer overflow and underflow historically caused severe vulnerabilities in smart contracts. The basic issue is that integers have a fixed range. If you exceed the maximum value, older compilers wrapped the value back to zero; if you went below zero on an unsigned integer, it wrapped to the maximum. Solidity 0.8 and later changed the default: common arithmetic operations now include built-in checks and will revert on overflow or underflow, preventing silent wrap-around. There are still cases to watch for: contracts compiled with older versions, manual unchecked blocks, or custom arithmetic logic can reintroduce wrapping behavior. A concise example is a counter stored as uint8 with value 255; executing count++ would cause a revert in Solidity 0.8+. The practical guidance is to prefer the default safe arithmetic, perform explicit range checks where needed, and use larger sizes like uint256 for counters where wrap-around is unlikely but still reasoned about. Always test boundary values and consider adding explicit require checks documenting intent. Misconception: people sometimes add gas-costly guards everywhere; instead, rely on compiler checks and add only the domain-specific guards you need. Final question to consider: when would an unchecked block be necessary, and how would you document its safety?

keyIdea.title: Safety
keyIdea.text: Solidity 0.8+ reverts on overflow by default. Test boundaries and avoid manual unchecked operations unless proven safe.

content.html:
Warning

Integer overflow and underflow

Understand default safety behavior and when explicit checks are necessary.

uint8 count = 255;
// In Solidity 0.8+, this will revert:
// count++;
Practical guidance
  • Rely on Solidity 0.8+ default checks for standard arithmetic.
  • Use require for domain-specific bounds and clear error messages.
  • Use unchecked blocks only when you fully audit and document the math operations to be safe.
Misconception

Assuming arithmetic always wraps silently. In modern Solidity, standard arithmetic reverts on overflow; wrapping must be intentionally used within unchecked blocks.

Pro Tip

Prefer uint256 for counters and token values unless you need a smaller type for packed storage. Test edge cases.

screens.title: The address Type and Payable
screens.subtitle: Representing accounts and sending Ether safely

narration.text: The address type in Solidity represents a 20-byte Ethereum account identifier. It can point to an externally owned account controlled by a private key or to a contract account. Addresses have useful members such as balance to inspect their Ether balance and low-level send or transfer operations. Importantly, to send Ether to an address you must use address payable or cast a plain address to payable. This distinction was added to make sending value explicit and safer. A common pattern is to store an owner address and mark it payable only when you intend to receive or forward Ether. For example, declaring owner as an address and recipient as address payable makes intent clear. Misconceptions arise when developers assume every address can accept Ether; only contracts with payable fallback functions or EOAs can receive Ether, and transferring to non-payable functions will revert. When designing contracts that move funds, be explicit about payable types and carefully handle reentrancy and error handling for transfers. Consider using call for sending Ether with gas management and always document who should be payable and why.

keyIdea.title: Address rule
keyIdea.text: Use address payable for accounts that must receive Ether; casting makes intent explicit and safer.

content.html:
Type Detail

address · address payable

A 20-byte identifier for EOAs and contracts. Use payable when the address must receive Ether.

address owner = 0xAbc1230000000000000000000000000000000000;
address payable recipient = payable(0xDef4560000000000000000000000000000000000);

// To transfer:
// recipient.transfer(amount);
Misconception

Not every contract can accept Ether. Ensure the recipient is payable and has a fallback or receive function if needed.

Practical advice
  • Declare payable only when receiving value is required.
  • Use call with gas controls and check return values to avoid unexpected failures.
  • Document which addresses are expected to be EOAs or contracts.
Key Takeaway

Make intent explicit: only mark addresses payable when the account must receive Ether.

screens.title: bytes and string — storage cost and fixed sizes
screens.subtitle: When to store raw data on-chain versus hashes off-chain

narration.text: bytes and string types handle binary and text data, but storing them on-chain is expensive. bytes represents a dynamically-sized byte array and string stores UTF-8 encoded text. When you know the exact number of bytes, fixed-size bytes1 through bytes32 are far more efficient because they fit into single storage words and can be packed. For larger data—images, documents, or long strings—you should store the content off-chain and keep a cryptographic hash, such as a bytes32 value produced by keccak256, on-chain to prove authenticity. A concrete example: computing keccak256 of a file and storing the resulting bytes32 hash dramatically reduces gas while preserving a verifiable anchor to off-chain content. A common mistake is to place long human-readable text on-chain out of convenience; this increases deployment and update costs. When you need to accept user-provided strings, prefer passing them as calldata in external functions to avoid extra copies into memory. Always weigh the tradeoffs between on-chain immutability and gas budgets, and choose fixed-size types where appropriate. bytes and string — storage cost and fixed sizes means use fixed-size bytes for known lengths and store large content off-chain with an on-chain hash for verification.. In practical terms, when to store raw data on-chain versus hashes off-chain. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Storage tip
keyIdea.text: Use fixed-size bytes for known lengths and store large content off-chain with an on-chain hash for verification.

content.html:
Type Detail

bytes · string

Prefer fixed-size bytes when length is known; avoid storing long strings directly on-chain.

bytes32 myHash = keccak256("hello");
string name = "Cohortia Course";
// Storing a large string is costly; consider storing only the hash on-chain.
Practical guideline
  • Use bytes1..bytes32 for fixed-size binary data.
  • Store hashes on-chain and larger payloads off-chain (for example, IPFS).
  • Accept strings via calldata in external functions to reduce copies.
Why it matters

Gas costs scale with stored bytes. Minimize on-chain payloads for lower deploy and transaction costs.

screens.title: Arrays: fixed-size, dynamic, storage vs memory
screens.subtitle: How to store, mutate, and avoid gas pitfalls

narration.text: Arrays provide ordered collections of same-typed elements, and Solidity supports both fixed-size and dynamic arrays. Fixed-size arrays declare a known length at compile time, while dynamic arrays can grow with push operations. Arrays can exist in three places: storage (persistent on-chain), memory (temporary during execution), and calldata (read-only function input for external calls). Storage arrays persist between transactions and are more expensive to modify; memory arrays are cheaper for temporary work but require copying data into memory. Calldata is the most gas-efficient for read-only external parameters because it avoids copying. A common mistake is to loop over very large dynamic storage arrays in a transaction — this can exceed gas limits. If you need to read many elements, prefer paginated reads off-chain or design indices and mappings for targeted access. Concrete example from the chapter: declare uint[] public ages and append using ages. push(_age) in a function. When iterating, consider reading only a slice or using mappings to avoid O(n) loops. Key takeaway: know where an array lives, and prefer patterns that minimize repeated on-chain iteration. Arrays: fixed-size, dynamic, storage vs memory means use calldata for read-only inputs, memory for temporary arrays, and avoid large on-chain loops in storage arrays.. In practical terms, how to store, mutate, and avoid gas pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Array strategy
keyIdea.text: Use calldata for read-only inputs, memory for temporary arrays, and avoid large on-chain loops in storage arrays.

content.html:
Reference Types

Arrays

Fixed-size vs dynamic, and the three storage locations: storage, memory, calldata.

uint[] public ages; // dynamic storage array

function addAge(uint _age) public {
  ages.push(_age);
}
Common mistake

Iterating through a very large storage array in a single transaction can exhaust gas. Design APIs to read pages or use mappings for direct lookup.

Practical patterns
  • Use calldata for external read-only arrays to avoid copies.
  • Use memory for local, temporary transformations.
  • Combine mapping for O(1) lookups with arrays if you need iteration and membership checks.
Key Takeaway

Memory and calldata provide cheaper, temporary storage. Minimize expensive storage loops.

screens.title: Structs for composite data
screens.subtitle: Grouping related values into a single state unit

narration.text: Structs let you group multiple fields under a single name, which is essential for modeling real-world entities in Solidity. For example, a User struct can hold an address, a name, a numeric score, and an isActive flag. Using a struct clarifies intent and reduces the number of separate state variables. Structs can be stored in mappings or arrays and accessed either as storage references or memory copies. A common pattern is to put structs in a mapping keyed by an address, providing O(1) access to a user's profile. When you read a struct from storage into a local variable without the storage keyword, you obtain a memory copy — modifications to that copy won’t persist. Always be explicit: use storage when you need to mutate and persist changes, and use memory for local read-only or temporary operations. One misconception is assuming struct field updates always persist when modifying a local copy. If you need to update fields, obtain a storage reference and then modify it. Overall, structs improve readability and ergonomics for complex state but require attention to storage semantics when mutating.

keyIdea.title: Struct use
keyIdea.text: Use structs to model complex entities and be explicit about storage vs memory when mutating fields.

content.html:
Reference Types

Structs

Group related variables into a named composite type for clearer state modeling.

struct User {
  address userAddress;
  string name;
  uint256 score;
  bool isActive;
}

User public admin; // state variable of type User
Mutation rules
  • Use storage to obtain a reference and persist changes.
  • Use memory for a temporary copy that won’t persist.
  • Always be explicit when assigning structs to avoid unintended non-persistent edits.
Misconception

Modifying a struct loaded into memory does not change storage. Use a storage reference for persisting updates.

screens.title: Mappings: efficient lookups, non-iterable
screens.subtitle: Key-value storage for O(1) access and patterns for iteration

narration.text: Mappings are Solidity's key-value store and provide efficient lookups for mappings from a key type to a value type. They are often used for balances, permissions, and registry-style data because reading or writing a mapping entry is essentially constant time. Mappings cannot be iterated or queried for size directly, which is a deliberate characteristic to keep storage efficient. If your contract needs to list all keys, you'll typically maintain a separate dynamic array of keys; however this adds gas cost every time you add or remove keys. Mappings allow value types as keys and any type as values, including structs and other mappings. This makes nested mappings useful for multi-dimensional lookups, for example mapping an address to another mapping of token IDs to balances. A common misuse is to expect mappings to behave like arrays. For practical code, use mapping(address => uint256) balances for O(1) membership checks, and if iteration is required, append the key to an auxiliary array while being mindful of the extra gas. The final question: can your design avoid iteration by shifting aggregation off-chain or using events for indexing?

keyIdea.title: Lookup rule
keyIdea.text: Use mappings for efficient existence checks and direct access; maintain a separate key list only when iteration is necessary.

content.html:
Reference Types

Mappings

Key-value stores for O(1) checks and direct access; not iterable by design.

mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

function updateBalance(address _user, uint256 _amount) public {
  balances[_user] = _amount;
}
Patterns
  • Use mapping for O(1) existence checks like mapping(address => bool) contributors.
  • If iteration is required, maintain an auxiliary array of keys and accept extra gas.
  • Consider emitting events for off-chain indexing rather than on-chain iteration.
Key Takeaway

Mappings are efficient but non-iterable. Use them for membership and lookups; move aggregation off-chain when possible.

screens.title: Visibility Specifiers
screens.subtitle: public, private, internal, external — access and autogenerated getters

narration.text: Visibility specifiers control where functions and state variables can be accessed from. Public items are accessible both internally and externally, and for state variables a public declaration automatically generates a getter function. Private items are restricted to the contract where they are declared and are not visible to derived contracts. Internal items are visible to the contract and any contracts that inherit from it; this is the default for state variables. External functions can only be called from outside the contract via transactions or other contracts — they are not callable internally using a plain function call. Choosing the right visibility is a security and design decision. If a function should only ever be used inside the contract, mark it private or internal. If a variable should not be exposed through a public getter, declare it private or internal and, if needed, provide a restricted accessor. A common mistake is leaving functions public by default and exposing functionality that should be internal. Always apply the least privilege principle: restrict visibility as much as possible and only open what you must. Consider adding explicit comments explaining why a public function is intentionally public to aid future auditors.

keyIdea.title: Access control
keyIdea.text: Restrict visibility with the least privilege principle; public automatically creates a getter for state variables.

content.html:
Access Control

public · private · internal · external

Choose visibility to limit exposure and manage inheritance behavior.

contract VisibilityExample {
  uint256 public publicVar = 10;
  uint256 private privateVar = 20;
  uint256 internal internalVar = 30;

  function externalFunction() external pure returns (string memory) {
    return "Called externally";
  }
}
Practical rules
  • Default state variable visibility is internal; make variables private when external access isn’t needed.
  • Use external for functions that are part of the contract's public interface and will be called from outside.
  • Document why a function is public to reduce accidental exposure during maintenance.
Common mistake

Leaving functions public by accident increases the attack surface. Prefer restrictive visibility by default.

screens.title: UserProfile Contract — Hands-on Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Implementing createUser, updateAge, and getUserProfile in Remix

narration.text: This walkthrough ties together the types and visibility rules into a small, testable contract. You will implement a User struct, a mapping from address to User, a boolean mapping to check existence, and three functions: createUser, updateAge, and getUserProfile. The createUser function uses a require guard to prevent duplicate profiles; this is an explicit safety check that reverts when someone tries to create more than one profile per account. updateAge ensures the profile exists before changing state, and getUserProfile is a public view function that returns the user's name, age and verification status. When deploying in Remix, compile with Solidity 0.8 or higher so arithmetic and other safety checks are enforced. Deploy to a local JavaScript VM and test by calling createUser from one account, reading the profile, updating the age, and then attempting a second createUser call from the same account to observe the revert. This exercise demonstrates structs, mappings, visibility, and require-based guards in a compact, realistic flow. As a reflection, notice how storing the struct in a mapping provides O(1) access while keeping iteration off-chain, and how explicit requires make failure modes intentional and testable.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on insight
keyIdea.text: A small contract demonstrates structs, mappings, visibility and guard clauses working together for predictable state changes.

content.html:
Lab Walkthrough

UserProfile.sol — Starter code

Terminal-style demo
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract UserProfile {
    // 1. Define a struct for a User profile
    struct User {
        string name;
        uint256 age;
        bool isVerified;
        address userAddress; // Store the user's address
    }

    // 2. Create a mapping to store User structs, keyed by their address
    mapping(address => User) public users;
    mapping(address => bool) public userExists; // To check if a user profile exists

    // 3. Implement a function to create a new user profile
    function createUser(string memory _name, uint256 _age) public {
        // Ensure a profile doesn't already exist for msg.sender
        require(!userExists[msg.sender], "User profile already exists.");

        users[msg.sender] = User(_name, _age, false, msg.sender);
        userExists[msg.sender] = true;
    }

    // 4. Implement a function to update a user's age
    function updateAge(uint256 _newAge) public {
        // Ensure the user profile exists
        require(userExists[msg.sender], "User profile does not exist.");

        users[msg.sender].age = _newAge;
    }

    // 5. Implement a function to get a user's profile details
    function getUserProfile(address _userAddress) public view returns (string memory, uint256, bool) {
        require(userExists[_userAddress], "User profile does not exist.");
        User storage user = users[_userAddress];
        return (user.name, user.age, user.isVerified);
    }
}
Walkthrough steps
  1. Compile with Solidity 0.8+ in Remix to get built-in arithmetic checks.
  2. Deploy to JavaScript VM and call createUser("Alice", 30) from account A.
  3. Call getUserProfile(accountA) to confirm stored values.
  4. Call updateAge(31) from account A and verify the change.
  5. Attempt createUser("Bob", 25) from the same account to observe the revert from require.
Why this matters

This short lab demonstrates secure defaults, mapping lookups, guard clauses and the difference between storage and memory in a real workflow.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from Solidity types and variables

narration.text: Keep these compact concepts in mind as you design contracts. First, value types are copied when assigned; reference types copy pointers. That affects correctness and gas. Second, choose types deliberately: use uint256 for balances, prefer fixed-size bytes when length is known, and avoid storing long strings on-chain. Third, mappings offer O(1) lookups but are not iterable — maintain auxiliary arrays only when iteration is strictly necessary. These three ideas—semantics, type choice, and lookup patterns—are the backbone of efficient Solidity design. Reflect on how each decision affects gas, readability, and security. When in doubt, write small tests that assert boundary behavior and visibility. These concepts will guide you when architecting contracts and choosing storage patterns. Key Concepts means value vs reference, careful type selection, and mapping patterns are the essential takeaways.. In practical terms, what to remember from solidity types and variables. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick memory
keyIdea.text: Value vs reference, careful type selection, and mapping patterns are the essential takeaways.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Value vs Reference
Copies vs pointers change semantics and gas. Choose with intent.
Type selection
Pick appropriate integer sizes, addresses and bytes for clarity and gas efficiency.
Mappings & patterns
Mappings are fast but non-iterable; maintain auxiliary structures only if iteration is required.
Summary takeaway

Design types and visibility with least privilege, test edge cases, and move heavy data off-chain to control gas and security.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for everyday Solidity development

narration.text: Remember these three practical reminders as you code: first, default to restrictive visibility and only publish what clients need; this reduces the attack surface. Second, avoid storing large data on-chain—store hashes or pointers and keep heavy payloads off-chain to manage gas. Third, always reason about storage location when mutating complex types: using a storage reference persists changes, while using a memory copy does not. These simple rules improve correctness, security, and cost predictability. When you plan a contract, map out where each piece of data will live, who can access it, and how frequently it will be written. That checklist will keep your implementations lean and auditable. What to Remember means restrict visibility, minimize on-chain payloads, and be explicit about storage versus memory when mutating state.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for everyday solidity development. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dev checklist
keyIdea.text: Restrict visibility, minimize on-chain payloads, and be explicit about storage versus memory when mutating state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What to Remember

What to Remember

Restrict Visibility
Use least privilege: make functions and variables as private as possible.
Minimize On-Chain Data
Store hashes or pointers, not large files or lengthy text, to control gas.
Be Explicit About Storage
Use storage for persistent changes and memory for temporary copies to avoid surprises.
Final reflection

Before you deploy, map data location, visibility, and gas cost for each state element. That planning prevents many common issues.
